# Sattakanipāta (AN 7)

**ID:** AN 7
**Section:** Aṅguttaranikāya (an)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Sattakanipāta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Book of the Sevens
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/an7

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sattakanipāta* ("The Book of the Sevens") constitutes the seventh numerical section of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* in the Sutta Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. It compiles discourses structured around sets of seven doctrinal concepts, spiritual qualities, types of persons, and illustrative similes [SuttaCentral]. Notable discourses include the *Satthusāsana Sutta* (AN 7.80/83), which sets forth for Upāli the core criteria for recognizing authentic Dhamma and Vinaya [Goodwin 2012]; the *Abyākatasutta* (AN 7.54), addressing the four unexplained questions concerning the post-mortem existence of the Tathāgata [Shulman 2014]; the *Pacalāyamānasutta* (AN 7.61), outlining antidotes to drowsiness and the conditions for the arising of all phenomena (*sabbe dhammā*) [SuttaCentral; Shulman 2014]; and the *Purisagatisutta* (AN 7.52/55), which describes five distinct subclasses of non-returners (*anāgāmī*) [Wen]. Other suttas examine insight into impermanence practiced by seven categories of individuals worthy of gifts (AN 7.16–17) [Wen], the practice of signless concentration (AN 7.53) [Wen], ancient shrines of the Vajjis (AN 7.19) [DeCaroli 2004], and balanced exertion for the welfare of oneself and others (AN 7.64) [Wangchuk 2007].

The collection possesses numerous parallels across early Buddhist literature. SuttaCentral identifies Chinese Āgama parallels for many suttas, especially in the *Madhyamāgama* (13 suttas) and *Ekottarikāgama* (9 suttas), as well as within the *Saṁyuktāgama* and individual Chinese sūtra translations [SuttaCentral]. Early Gāndhārī manuscript fragments parallel specific discourses such as AN 7.71, illustrating the modular, formulaic transmission of early sūtra texts [Salomon 2018]. In Pali-internal reuse, DharmaNexus detects significant textual sharing with other books of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (notably AN 5, AN 4, AN 10, and AN 6) and the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16, which shares passages with AN 7.22) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages with Sanskrit works such as the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, and Sanskrit *Ekottarāgama* fragments, as well as Tibetan canonical texts including Śamathadeva’s *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopāyikā* (D4094), the *Lokaprajñapti* (D4086), and the *Vinayavastu* [DharmaNexus]. An early romanized edition was prepared by E. Hardy for the Pali Text Society [Bendall 1893], and comparative philological research relies on discourses like AN 7.65 to elucidate translation variants in Chinese Āgama texts [Meisig 2010].
